extracted.intended_audience: authors seeking sensitivity or expert readers; writers aiming to create authentic, inclusive representation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using sensitivity readers and expert/targeted beta readers to ensure authentic, inclusive narratives and avoid harmful stereotypes; includes what sensitivity readers check and how expert readers contribute subject-matter detail. Useful for authors preparing manuscripts that feature characters, cultures, identities, or specialized knowledge outside the author's lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for sensitivity readers / representation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing has a diversity problem: the industry itself is overwhelmingly white, and most of the books being published are the products of white authors or feature primarily white characters. Representation matters deeply. Authors have a remarkable chance to help turn the tide on these dismal numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites statistics (e.g., 31% of children’s books in 2017 were about non-white characters but only 7% were written by Black, Latinx, or Native American authors) and points to external resources (#representationmatters on Twitter, Geena Davis' work, USC report). Use sensitivity readers to address this industry imbalance and improve representation in your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of a sensitivity reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitivity readers provide nuanced feedback that will change your writing for the better—and make sure that you're helping with representation, not becoming part of the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity readers operate as part of an author's toolkit to identify and correct problematic elements in manuscript text. They help ensure inclusion and prevent harm, not just point out errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of sensitivity reading (what sensitivity readers check)
rubrics_metrics.description: Microaggressions, word choice, accuracy, and racist/sexist tropes all fall under the umbrella of a sensitivity reader's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should expect sensitivity readers to evaluate language, implied attitudes, factual accuracy about identities/experiences, and recurring harmful or stereotypical narrative patterns. The FAQ frames these as the core domains a sensitivity reader will address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of an expert (targeted beta) reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Also known as 'targeted beta readers,' these readers are people who have backgrounds or experiences in the things you're writing about. They will help you catch small details that will make your writing feel even more authentic and deep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert readers are appropriate when the manuscript contains subject-matter details (e.g., a character who adores horses). Use expert readers to verify domain-specific facts, lived-experience nuance, and small but telling details that lend authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match reader experience to manuscript needs / vetted reader selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Salt & Sage Books has a collection of vetted readers for you to choose from with a broad array of experiences. See the Sensitivity & Expert Reader page for their profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sensitivity/expert readers whose lived experience or professional expertise aligns with the identities, cultures, or specialized knowledge represented in your manuscript. The service emphasizes vetted profiles so authors can choose appropriate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use sensitivity/expert readers
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to do something about representation (i.e., improve inclusion and reduce harm), sensitivity readers are recommended; they are quickly becoming an essential part of every author's arsenal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors writing outside their lived experience or addressing marginalized identities should engage sensitivity and/or expert readers as a standard part of their revision process. The page frames this as both ethical and practical—improving authenticity and reducing the risk of perpetuating stereotypes.
